paragraphs: There was once a learned gentleman appointed to examine the archives of Southminster Cathedral and report on them. This would take a considerable amount of time, so he decided to find lodgings in the city. The cathedral authorities offered him generous hospitality, but Mr. Lake felt he would rather have his day to himself. They accepted this as reasonable. Eventually the Dean wrote advising him, if he had not yet found anything suitable, to contact Mr. Worby, the head verger. He lived conveniently close to the church and was willing to take a quiet lodger for three or four weeks. This was exactly the arrangement Mr. Lake wanted. They easily agreed on terms, and early in December the investigator found himself, like another Mr. Datchery, as he remarked to himself, occupying a very comfortable room in an ancient house full of “cathedral character”.

A man so familiar with cathedral customs, and treated with such obvious consideration by the Dean and Chapter of this particular cathedral, could hardly fail to earn the head verger’s respect. Mr. Worby even accepted some corrections to statements he had been making to groups of visitors for years. For his part, Mr. Lake found the verger a very cheerful companion, and took every opportunity to enjoy a conversation with him when the day’s work was over.

One evening, at about nine o’clock, Mr. Worby knocked at his lodger’s door. “I have to go across to the cathedral, Mr. Lake,” he said, “and I think I promised that the next time I did, I’d give you the chance to see what it looks like at night. It’s quite fine and dry outside, if you’d care to come.”
“Of course I will. Thank you very much for thinking of it, Mr. Worby. Just let me get my coat.”
“Here it is, sir, and I’ve another lantern here. You’ll find you need it on the steps, as there’s no moon.”
“Anyone might think we were Jasper and Durdles all over again, mightn’t they?” said Lake as they crossed the cathedral close, for he had found out that the verger had read Edwin Drood.

“Well, they might,” said Mr. Worby with a short laugh, “though I don’t know whether we ought to take it as a compliment. They had odd ways at that cathedral, I often think. Doesn’t it seem so to you, sir? A full choral morning service at seven o’clock, all year round. That wouldn’t suit our boys’ voices nowadays, and I think one or two of the men would ask for a pay rise if the Chapter brought it in—especially the altos.”
They had reached the south-west door. As Mr. Worby unlocked it, Lake said, “Have you ever found anyone accidentally locked in here?”

“Twice. One was a drunken sailor. How he got in, I don’t know. I suppose he fell asleep during the service, but by the time I reached him he was praying loudly enough to bring the roof down. Lord, what a noise that man made! He said it was the first time he’d been inside a church for ten years, and swore he’d never try it again. The other was an old sheep. That was the boys, playing their games. It was the last time they tried that, though. There, sir, now you can see what we look like. Our late Dean used to bring groups in now and then, but he preferred a moonlit night. There was a bit of poetry he would quote to them, about a Scottish cathedral, I understand. But I don’t know: I almost think the effect is better when it’s all dark. It seems to add to the size and height. Now, if you don’t mind waiting somewhere in the nave while I go up into the choir, where I have my business, you’ll see what I mean.”

Lake accordingly waited, leaning against a pillar. He watched the light wavering along the length of the church and up the steps into the choir, until some screen or piece of furniture blocked it. Only its reflection on the pillars and roof remained visible. A few minutes later Worby reappeared at the choir entrance and waved his lantern, signalling to Lake to join him.

“I suppose it is Worby, and not a substitute,” Lake thought as he walked up the nave. In fact, nothing was wrong. Worby showed him the papers he had come to fetch from the Dean’s stall and asked what he thought of the sight. Lake agreed that it was well worth seeing. “I suppose,” he said, as they walked together towards the altar steps, “you’re too used to walking about here at night to feel nervous. But you must get a fright now and then, mustn’t you, when a book falls or a door swings shut?”

“No, Mr. Lake, I can’t say I think much about noises, not nowadays. I’m much more afraid of finding a gas leak or a burst stove pipe than anything else. Still, there have been times, years ago. Did you notice that plain altar-tomb there? We say it’s fifteenth-century; I don’t know if you agree. Well, if you didn’t look at it, just come back and give it a glance, if you would be so good.” It stood on the north side of the choir, rather awkwardly placed, only about three feet from the stone screen around the choir. As the verger had said, it was quite plain, apart from some ordinary stone panelling. The only feature of interest was a fairly large metal cross on the north side, the side next to the screen.

Lake agreed that it could be no earlier than the Perpendicular Gothic period. “But,” he said, “unless it’s the tomb of some remarkable person, you’ll forgive me for saying I don’t think it’s particularly noteworthy.”

“Well, I can’t say it’s the tomb of anyone noted in history,” said Worby with a dry smile, “because we haven’t any record at all of who it was built for. All the same, if you’ve half an hour to spare, sir, when we get back to the house, Mr. Lake, I could tell you a tale about that tomb. I won’t begin now. It’s cold here, and we don’t want to stand about all night.”
“Of course. I’d be immensely interested to hear it.”

“Very well, sir, you shall. Now, if I might ask you a question,” he went on as they passed down the choir aisle, “in our little local guide—and not only there, but in the little book about our cathedral in that series—you’ll find it says this part of the building was put up before the twelfth century. Now, of course, I’d be glad enough to agree, but—mind the step, sir—but I ask you: does the way the stone is laid in this part of the wall”—he tapped it with his key—“does it look to you like what you might call Saxon masonry? No, I thought not. Nor does it to me. Now, if you’ll believe me, I’ve told those men as much fifty times if I’ve told them once. One’s the librarian of our Free Library here, and the other came down from London specially. But I might just as well have talked to that bit of stonework. Still, there it is. I suppose everyone has their opinions.”

Mr. Worby continued discussing this peculiar feature of human nature almost until they went back into his house. The state of the fire in Lake’s sitting room prompted him to suggest finishing the evening in his own parlour. There we find them settled a short time later.

Mr. Worby made a long story of it, and I will not attempt to tell it entirely in his own words or in his own order. Immediately afterwards, Lake wrote down the substance of what he had heard, together with a few passages that had lodged in his memory word for word. I shall probably find it best to condense Lake’s account to some extent.

Mr. Worby, it appeared, had been born around 1828. His father had been connected with the cathedral before him, and so had his grandfather. One or both had been choristers. Later in life they had both worked on the building, one as a mason and the other as a carpenter. Worby himself, although he frankly admitted that his voice was nothing special, had been recruited into the choir at about ten years old.

It was in 1840 that the wave of the Gothic Revival struck Southminster Cathedral. “A lot of lovely things went then, sir,” said Worby with a sigh. “My father could hardly believe it when he got his orders to clear out the choir. A new dean had just arrived—Dean Burscough. My father had served his apprenticeship with a good firm of joiners in the city, and he knew good work when he saw it. Cruel, he used to call it. All that beautiful oak panelling, as good as the day it was put up, with garlands of leaves and fruit, and lovely old gilding on the coats of arms and the organ pipes. It all went to the timber yard. Every bit, except some little pieces worked into the Lady Chapel, and here in this overmantel. Well, I may be wrong, but I say our choir has never looked as good since. Still, they found out a lot about the history of the church, and there’s no doubt it needed repairing. Very few winters went by without us losing a pinnacle.” Mr. Lake agreed with Worby’s views on restoration, but admits that by this point he feared they might never reach the actual story. Perhaps his manner showed it.

Worby hurried to reassure him. “Not that I couldn’t talk about that subject for hours at a time. I do, when I get the chance. But Dean Burscough was very keen on the Gothic period, and nothing would satisfy him unless everything was made to match it. One morning he arranged for my father to meet him in the choir after the service. He came back after taking off his robes in the vestry, carrying a roll of paper. The verger we had then brought in a table, and they started spreading it out, putting prayer books on it to hold it down. My father helped them, and he saw it was a picture of the inside of a cathedral choir. The Dean—he was a quick-spoken gentleman—says, ‘Well, Worby, what do you think of that?’ ‘Why,’ says my father, ‘I don’t think I have the pleasure of knowing that view. Would that be Hereford Cathedral, Mr. Dean?’ ‘No, Worby,’ says the Dean, ‘that is Southminster Cathedral as we hope to see it before many years have passed.’ ‘Indeed, sir,’ says my father. And that was all he said—at least to the Dean. But he used to tell me he felt quite faint when he looked round our choir, all comfortable and furnished, as I remember it, and then saw this nasty little lifeless picture, as he called it, drawn by some London architect. Well, there I go again. But you’ll see what I mean if you look at this old view.”

Worby took a framed print down from the wall. “Well, the long and short of it was that the Dean gave my father a copy of an order from the Chapter. He was to clear everything out of the choir—make a clean sweep—ready for the new work being designed in London. And he was to start as soon as he could get the demolition men together. Now then, sir, if you look at that picture, you’ll see where the pulpit used to stand. That’s what I want you to notice, please.” It was certainly easy to see: an unusually large wooden structure with a domed sounding-board above it. It stood at the east end of the stalls on the north side of the choir, facing the bishop’s throne. Worby went on to explain that during the alterations, services were held in the nave. This disappointed the choir members, who had been expecting a holiday. The organist, in particular, was suspected of deliberately damaging the workings of the temporary organ, which had been hired from London at considerable expense.

Demolition began with the choir screen and organ loft, and gradually moved eastwards. As Worby said, it revealed many interesting details of earlier work. While this was going on, the members of the Chapter naturally spent a great deal of time in and around the choir. The elder Worby could not help overhearing some of their conversation. It soon became clear to him that there must have been considerable disagreement, especially among the senior Canons, before they adopted the policy now being carried out. Some thought they would catch their deaths of cold in the stalls across the end of the choir, with no screen to protect them from draughts through the nave. Others objected to being visible to people in the choir aisles, especially during sermons. They said they found it helpful to listen in a position that people might misunderstand. The strongest opposition came from their oldest member, who objected to removing the pulpit until the very last moment. “You ought not to touch it, Mr. Dean,” he said emphatically one morning as the two stood before it. “You don’t know what harm you may do.” “Harm? It’s not a piece of work with any particular merit, Canon.” “Don’t call me Canon,” the old man said sharply. “That is, I have been known as Dr. Ayloff for thirty years, and I should be obliged, Mr. Dean, if you would kindly humour me in that respect. As for the pulpit, which I’ve preached from for thirty years—though I don’t insist on that—all I’ll say is, I know you’re doing wrong in moving it.” “But what sense would there be, my dear Doctor, in leaving it where it is when we’re fitting out the rest of the choir in a completely different style? What reason could we give, apart from the look of the thing?” “Reason! Reason!” said old Dr. Ayloff. “If you young men—if I may say that without disrespect, Mr. Dean—if you would only listen to reason a little, instead of always asking for it, we should get on better. But there, I’ve said my piece.” The old gentleman hobbled away and, as it turned out, never entered the cathedral again. It was a hot summer, and suddenly illness became widespread. Dr. Ayloff was among the first to die, from some condition of the chest muscles that attacked him painfully at night. At many services there were very few of the choirmen and boys present.

Meanwhile, the pulpit had been removed. In fact, its sounding-board had been taken down within an hour or two of Dr. Ayloff’s protest. Part of it still survives as a table in a summer house in the palace garden. Removing the base took considerable trouble, but revealed an altar-tomb, to the great delight of the supporters of restoration. It was, of course, the tomb Worby had pointed out to Lake that very evening. A great deal of fruitless research went into attempts to identify its occupant. From that day to this, no one has been able to put a name to him. The tomb had been very carefully boxed in beneath the pulpit’s base, so what little decoration it had was undamaged. Only on the north side was there something that looked like damage: a gap between two of the slabs that formed the side. It was perhaps two or three inches wide. Palmer, the mason, was told to fill it in a week later, when he came to do some other small jobs near that part of the choir.

It was certainly a very difficult season. Someone suggested that the church had been built on what was once a marsh. Whether that was the reason or not, many of those living immediately around it found little pleasure in the exquisite sunny days and calm nights of August and September. For several older people, including Dr. Ayloff, as we have seen, the summer proved fatal. Even among the younger people, few escaped either several weeks in bed or, at the very least, a brooding sense of oppression accompanied by hateful nightmares. Gradually a suspicion took shape, and grew into a conviction: the alterations to the cathedral had something to do with it. The widow of an old former verger, who received a pension from the Chapter of Southminster, had dreams that she described to her friends. In them, a shape slipped out of the little door in the south transept as darkness fell. It flitted about the cathedral close, going in a different direction each night, disappearing for a while into one house after another and finally coming out again as the night sky grew pale. She could see nothing of it, she said, except that it was a moving form. But she had an impression that when it returned to the church, as it seemed to do at the end of the dream, it turned its head. Then, although she could not say why, she thought it had red eyes. Worby remembered hearing her tell this dream at a tea party in the chapter clerk’s house. The fact that it kept recurring might perhaps be seen as a sign of approaching illness, he said. At any rate, before the end of September the old lady was in her grave.

Interest in the restoration of this great church extended beyond its own county. One day that summer, a Fellow of the Society of Antiquaries, a man of some reputation, visited it. He had come to write an account of the discoveries for the Society, and his wife, who accompanied him, was to make a series of drawings to illustrate his report. In the morning she made a general sketch of the choir. In the afternoon she turned to details. First she drew the newly uncovered altar-tomb. When she had finished, she pointed out to her husband a beautiful piece of repeating patterned ornament on the screen just behind it. Like the tomb, it had been completely hidden by the pulpit. Of course, he said, they must have a drawing of that. So she sat down on the tomb and began a careful drawing that kept her occupied until dusk.

By this time her husband had finished measuring and describing things, and they agreed it was time to return to their hotel. “You might as well brush my skirt, Frank,” she said. “I’m sure it must be covered in dust.” He dutifully obeyed, but after a moment he said, “I don’t know whether you particularly value this dress, my dear, but I’m inclined to think it’s seen its best days. A great piece of it is gone.” “Gone? Where?” she said. “I don’t know where it’s gone, but it’s missing from the bottom edge, here at the back.” She hastily pulled the skirt round to look, and was horrified to find a jagged tear extending some way up into the fabric. It looked very much, she said, as though a dog had torn it away. In any case, the dress was hopelessly ruined, much to her annoyance. Although they searched everywhere, they could not find the missing piece. They concluded that the damage could have happened in many ways, for the choir was full of old pieces of woodwork with nails sticking out. In the end, they could only suppose that one of these had caused it, and that the workmen, who had been there all day, had carried off that particular piece of wood with the torn fabric still attached.

Worby thought it was about this time that his little dog began to look anxious as the hour approached for it to be put in the shed in the back yard. His mother had ruled that it must not sleep in the house. One evening, he said, as he was about to pick it up and carry it out, it looked at him “like a human being, and waved its hand, I was going to say. Well, you know how they carry on sometimes. It ended with me putting it under my coat and hurrying it upstairs, and I’m afraid I more or less deceived my poor mother about it. After that the dog became very clever at hiding under the bed for half an hour or more before bedtime, and we managed things so my mother never found out what we’d done.” Of course, Worby was glad of its company in any case, but especially when the disturbance still remembered in Southminster as “the crying” began.

“Night after night,” said Worby, “that dog seemed to know it was coming. He would creep out and snuggle into the bed, cuddling right up to me and shivering. When the crying came, he’d be like a wild thing, pushing his head under my arm, and I was almost as bad. We’d hear it six or seven times, no more. When he brought his head out again, I knew it was over for that night. What was it like, sir? Well, I’ve only ever heard one thing that seemed to describe it properly. I happened to be playing in the close when two of the Canons met and said good morning to one another. ‘Sleep well last night?’ says one. That was Mr. Henslow, and the other was Mr. Lyall. ‘Can’t say I did,’ says Mr. Lyall. ‘Rather too much of Isaiah 34:14 for me.’ ‘34:14?’ says Mr. Henslow. ‘What’s that?’ ‘You call yourself a Bible reader!’ says Mr. Lyall. You must understand, Mr. Henslow was one of what they used to call Simeon’s lot—more or less what we’d call the Evangelical party. ‘Go and look it up.’ I wanted to know what he meant, so I ran home and got out my own Bible. And there it was: ‘The satyr will cry to his fellow.’ Well, I thought, is that what we’ve been listening to these last few nights? I tell you, it made me look over my shoulder once or twice. Of course, I’d already asked my father and mother what it could be, but both said it was most likely cats. They answered very shortly, though, and I could see they were troubled. My word, that was a noise! It sounded hungry, as if it was calling for someone who wouldn’t come. If ever you felt you wanted company, it was while you waited for it to begin again. I believe they put men on watch in different parts of the close for two or three nights. But they always gathered together in one corner, as near to the High Street as they could get, and nothing came of it.

“Well, the next thing was this. Another boy and I had gone up into the close after morning service. He’s a grocer in the city now, as his father was before him. We heard old Palmer, the mason, bellowing at some of his men. So we went nearer, because we knew he was a grumpy old fellow and there might be some fun. It turned out that Palmer had told this man to fill the gap in that old tomb. The man kept saying he’d done it as well as he could, and Palmer was carrying on like a man possessed. ‘You call that doing a job?’ he says. ‘You deserve the sack for this. What do you think I pay your wages for? What do you think I’m going to say to the Dean and Chapter when they come round—which they might do at any time—and see where you’ve been bungling about, covering the whole place with mess and plaster and Lord knows what?’ ‘Well, master, I did the best I could,’ says the man. ‘I don’t know any more than you do how it came to fall out like this. I packed it right into the hole,’ he says, ‘and now it’s fallen out. I’ve never seen anything like it.’

“‘Fallen out?’ says old Palmer. ‘Why, it’s nowhere near the place. Blown out, you mean.’ He picked up a piece of plaster lying against the screen, three or four feet away, and so did I. It wasn’t dry yet. Old Palmer looked at it in a curious way, then turned to me and said, ‘Now then, you boys, have you been playing your games here?’ ‘No,’ I says, ‘I haven’t, Mr. Palmer. None of us has been anywhere near here until this minute.’ While I was speaking, the other boy, Evans, started looking in through the gap. I heard him draw in his breath, and he pulled away quickly and came up to us. ‘I believe there’s something in there,’ he says. ‘I saw something shiny.’ ‘What? I dare say,’ says old Palmer. ‘Well, I haven’t time to hang about here. William, go and get some more stuff and do the job properly this time. If you don’t, there’ll be trouble in my yard.’

“So the man went away, and so did Palmer. We boys stayed behind, and I said to Evans, ‘Did you really see something in there?’ ‘Yes,’ he says, ‘I really did.’ Then I said, ‘Let’s push something in and stir it up.’ We tried several bits of wood lying about, but they were all too big. Then Evans had a sheet of music he’d brought with him—an anthem or a service, I forget which now—and he rolled it up small and pushed it into the gap. He did it two or three times, and nothing happened. ‘Give it here, boy,’ I said, and I had a try. No, nothing happened. Then—I’m sure I don’t know why I thought of it—I bent down right opposite the gap, put two fingers in my mouth and whistled. You know the way. At that, I thought I seemed to hear something moving, and I said to Evans, ‘Come away. I don’t like this.’ ‘Oh, rubbish,’ he says. ‘Give me that roll.’ He took it and pushed it in. I don’t think I’ve ever seen anyone turn as pale as he did. ‘I say, Worby,’ he says, ‘it’s caught, or else someone has hold of it.’ ‘Pull it out or leave it,’ I says. ‘Come on, let’s go.’ He gave it a good pull and it came away. At least, most of it did. The end was gone, torn off. Evans looked at it for a second, then made a sort of croaking noise and dropped it. We both got out of there as fast as we could. When we were outside, Evans said, ‘Did you see the end of that paper?’ ‘No,’ I said, ‘only that it was torn.’ ‘Yes, it was,’ he says, ‘but it was wet too, and black!’ Well, partly because we’d had such a fright, and partly because that music was needed in a day or two and we knew there would be a row with the organist, we didn’t tell anyone else. I suppose the workmen swept up what was left with the rest of the rubbish. But if you asked Evans this very day, he’d insist he saw that paper wet and black at the torn end.”

After that the boys kept well away from the choir, so Worby was unsure how the mason’s next attempt to mend the tomb had turned out. But from scraps of conversation among workmen passing through the choir, he gathered that they had met with some difficulty, and that the boss, Mr. Palmer himself, had tried his hand at it. A little later he happened to see Mr. Palmer knocking at the Deanery door and being let in by the butler. A day or so after that, something his father said at breakfast told him that a rather unusual job was to be done in the cathedral after morning service the following day. “And I’d just as soon it was today,” his father added. “I don’t see the use of taking risks.” “ ‘Father,’ I said, ‘what are you going to do in the cathedral tomorrow?’ He turned on me as fiercely as I ever saw him. My poor father was a wonderfully good-tempered man as a rule. ‘My lad,’ he says, ‘I’ll ask you not to listen in to the conversation of your elders and betters. It’s bad manners, and it’s dishonest. What I’m going to do or not do in the cathedral tomorrow is none of your business. If I catch sight of you hanging about there tomorrow after your work is done, I’ll send you home with a sharp telling-off. Now remember that.’ Of course I said I was very sorry and so on. And equally of course, I went off and made my plans with Evans. We knew there was a staircase in the corner of the transept that led up to the triforium gallery. In those days its door was almost always open, and even if it wasn’t, we knew the key was usually under a piece of matting nearby. So we decided that next morning we would be putting away music and so on while the other boys left. Then we’d slip up the stairs and watch from the gallery for any sign of work going on.

“Well, that very night I dropped off to sleep as soundly as boys do, and suddenly the dog woke me by coming into the bed. Now we’re going to get it badly, I thought, for he seemed more frightened than usual. After about five minutes, sure enough, the cry came. I can’t give you any idea of what it was like. And so close, too—closer than I’d heard it yet. Here’s a curious thing, Mr. Lake: you know how sounds echo in this close, especially if you stand on this side. Well, that crying never gave the slightest echo at all. But, as I said, it was terribly close that night. And on top of the fright I got from hearing it, I had another, because I heard something rustling outside in the passage. Now I really thought I was done for. But I noticed the dog seemed to perk up a little. Then someone whispered outside the door, and I very nearly laughed aloud, because I knew it was my father and mother, who’d got out of bed because of the noise. ‘Whatever is it?’ says my mother. ‘Hush! I don’t know,’ says my father, sounding agitated. ‘Don’t disturb the boy. I hope he didn’t hear anything.’

“Knowing they were just outside made me bolder, and I slipped out of bed and across to my little window, which looked onto the close. The dog burrowed right down to the bottom of the bed. I looked out. At first I couldn’t see anything. Then, down in the shadow under a buttress, I made out what I shall always say were two red spots. A dull red, nothing like a lamp or a fire, but just enough to pick them out from the black shadow. I had only just seen them when it appeared we weren’t the only people who had been disturbed. I saw a window light up in a house on the left, and the light moving. I turned my head for a moment to make sure, then looked back into the shadow for those two red things. They were gone. However much I peered and stared, there wasn’t another sign of them. Then I had my last fright that night. Something touched my bare leg. But that was all right: it was my little dog, who had got out of bed and was prancing about, making a great fuss, only keeping quiet. Seeing that he was quite cheerful again, I took him back to bed, and we slept for the rest of the night!

“Next morning I managed to tell my mother I’d had the dog in my room. After everything she’d said about it before, I was surprised how calmly she took it. ‘Did you?’ she says. ‘Well, by rights you ought to go without breakfast for doing that behind my back. But I don’t know that any great harm has been done. Only ask my permission next time, do you hear?’ A little later I said something to my father about hearing the cats again. ‘Cats?’ he says, and looked across at my poor mother. She coughed, and he said, ‘Oh! Ah! Yes, cats. I believe I heard them myself.’

“It was a curious morning altogether. Nothing seemed to go right. The organist stayed in bed. The minor Canon forgot it was the nineteenth day of the month and waited for the singing of ‘Come, let us sing’. After a while the deputy began playing the chant for evensong, which was in a minor key. Then the boys on the Dean’s side of the choir were laughing so much they couldn’t sing. When we reached the anthem, the solo boy got the giggles, pretended his nose was bleeding, and pushed the book at me. I hadn’t practised the solo part, and even if I’d known it, I wasn’t much of a singer. Well, things were rougher fifty years ago, you see, and I got a pinch from the counter-tenor behind me that I remembered.

“Somehow we got through it. Neither the men nor the boys wanted to wait and see whether the Canon in residence—Mr. Henslow—would come to the vestries and fine them. I don’t believe he did. For one thing, I fancy he’d read the wrong lesson for the first time in his life, and knew it. Anyway, Evans and I had no difficulty slipping up the stairs, as I told you. When we reached the top, we lay flat on our stomachs where we could just put our heads out above the old tomb. We had barely done so when we heard the verger we had then shutting the iron porch gates and locking the south-west door, and then the transept door. So we knew something was happening, and that they meant to keep the public out for a while.

“Next, the Dean and the Canon came in through their door on the north side. Then I saw my father and old Palmer, with a couple of their best men. Palmer stood talking with the Dean for a while in the middle of the choir. He had a coil of rope, and the men had crowbars. They all looked a little nervous. So there they stood talking, and at last I heard the Dean say, ‘Well, I have no time to waste, Palmer. If you think this will satisfy the people of Southminster, I’ll allow it to be done. But I must say that never in my life have I heard such utter nonsense from a practical man as I’ve heard from you. Don’t you agree, Henslow?’ As far as I could hear, Mr. Henslow said something like, ‘Oh! Well, we’re told not to judge others, aren’t we, Mr. Dean?’ The Dean gave a sort of sniff and walked straight up to the tomb. He stood behind it with his back to the screen, and the others edged up rather cautiously. Henslow stopped on the south side and scratched his chin. Then the Dean spoke up. ‘Palmer,’ he says, ‘which would be easier: taking off the top slab, or moving one of the side slabs?’

“Old Palmer and his men pottered about for a while, looking round the edge of the top slab and tapping the sides—south, east, west, everywhere except the north. Henslow said something about it being better to try the south side, because there was more light and more room to move. Then my father, who had been watching, went round to the north side. He knelt down and felt the slab beside the gap, then stood up, dusted his knees, and said to the Dean, ‘Beg your pardon, Mr. Dean, but I think if Mr. Palmer tries this slab, he’ll find it comes out easily enough. It seems to me one of the men could prise it out by putting his crowbar into this gap.’ ‘Ah! Thank you, Worby,’ says the Dean. ‘That’s a good suggestion. Palmer, let one of your men do that, will you?’

“So the man came round, put his bar in and pressed on it. At that very moment, when they were all bending over and we boys had our heads well out over the edge of the gallery, there was a most dreadful crash at the west end of the choir. It sounded as though a whole stack of heavy timber had fallen down a flight of stairs. Well, you can’t expect me to tell you everything that happened in that one moment. Of course, there was a terrible commotion. I heard the slab fall out and the crowbar hit the floor, and I heard the Dean say, ‘Good God!’

“When I looked down again, I saw the Dean sprawled on the floor. The men were hurrying away down the choir. Henslow was just about to help the Dean up, Palmer was going to stop the men, as he said afterwards, and my father was sitting on the altar step with his face in his hands. The Dean was very cross. ‘I wish to goodness you’d look where you’re going, Henslow,’ he says. ‘Why you should all take to your heels when a stick of wood falls down, I cannot imagine.’ Henslow kept explaining that he had been right over on the other side of the tomb, but nothing would satisfy the Dean.

“Then Palmer came back and reported that there was nothing to account for the noise, and apparently nothing had fallen down. When the Dean had finished feeling himself over, they gathered round the tomb—all except my father, who stayed where he was. Someone lit a piece of candle, and they looked inside. ‘Nothing there,’ says the Dean. ‘What did I tell you? Wait! Here’s something. What’s this? A bit of music paper and a piece of torn fabric—part of a dress, it looks like. Both quite modern. Of no interest whatever. Perhaps another time you’ll take the advice of an educated man.’ Or something like that. And off he went, limping a little, and out through the north door. As he left, though, he called back angrily to Palmer for leaving the door open. Palmer called out, ‘Very sorry, sir,’ but shrugged his shoulders. Henslow said, ‘I fancy the Dean is mistaken. I shut the door behind me, but he’s a little upset.’ Then Palmer said, ‘Why, where’s Worby?’ They saw him sitting on the step and went up to him. He seemed to be recovering, and was wiping his forehead. Palmer helped him to his feet, which I was glad to see.

“They were too far away for me to hear what they said, but my father pointed to the north door in the aisle. Palmer and Henslow both looked very surprised and frightened. After a while my father and Henslow left the church. The others hurried as much as they could to put the slab back and plaster it in. At about twelve o’clock, as the clock struck, the cathedral opened again, and we boys got home as quickly as we could.

“I was desperate to know what had given my poor father such a fright. When I got home and found him sitting in his chair with a glass of spirits, and my mother standing beside him looking anxious, I couldn’t help blurting out where I’d been. But he didn’t seem upset by it, not in the sense of losing his temper. ‘You were there, were you? Well, did you see it?’ ‘I saw everything, Father,’ I said, ‘except when the noise came.’ ‘Did you see what knocked the Dean over?’ he says. ‘The thing that came out of the monument? You didn’t? Well, that’s a mercy.’ ‘Why, what was it, Father?’ I said. ‘Come, you must have seen it,’ he says. ‘Didn’t you see? A thing like a man, covered all over with hair, and with two great eyes?’

“Well, that was all I could get out of him then. Later he seemed ashamed of having been so frightened, and used to put me off when I asked about it. But years afterwards, when I was a grown man, we talked more about it from time to time. He always said the same thing. ‘It was black,’ he’d say, ‘and a mass of hair, and it had two legs, and the light caught its eyes.’

“Well, that’s the tale of that tomb, Mr. Lake. It’s one we don’t tell our visitors, and I’d be obliged if you didn’t make any use of it until I’m gone. I suspect Mr. Evans will feel the same way, if you ask him.”

So it proved. But more than twenty years have passed, and the grass is growing over both Worby and Evans. Mr. Lake therefore felt no difficulty in passing his notes, taken in 1890, on to me. With them he sent a sketch of the tomb and a copy of the short inscription on the metal cross fixed to the centre of its north side at Dr. Lyall’s expense. It came from the Vulgate version of Isaiah 34, and its three Latin words meant—
THERE THE NIGHT-MONSTER LAY.
